mcqs.question: A candidate opens a "design a live comments feed" frontend round by sketching a load balancer and a consistent-hashing shard map. What's the most accurate read on this move?
options: It's the correct opening — frontend and backend HLD use the identical first step
It imports the wrong framework — the round is testing component boundaries, state ownership, and UI behavior under a flaky client network, not server-side scaling
It's fine as long as they eventually draw a component tree too
It's wrong only because load balancers are a security topic, not a scaling topic
mcqs.explanation: Frontend system design optimizes for perceived speed and correctness on a device and network you don't control; a load balancer answers a backend question the interviewer isn't asking. Doing both eventually doesn't fix opening with the wrong framework — the first few minutes set the interviewer's read on you.

mcqs.question: Why is naming devices, scale, offline needs, and real-time-ness in the first few minutes worth more than an early diagram?
options: Because interviewers deduct points for any diagram drawn before minute 10
Because these answers change the architecture itself, so drawing first risks a detailed design for the wrong problem
Because component trees are only needed for desktop-only products
Because real-time-ness determines the programming language you should use
mcqs.explanation: A mobile-first, offline-tolerant feed and an internal admin tool's feed are different designs entirely, even though both are "a feed" — scoping first prevents a detailed, well-drawn answer to the wrong requirements. None of the distractors reflect why the ordering matters.

mcqs.question: Two components on the same page disagree about whether a post has been liked. What does the data-flow step (step 3) say is the most likely root cause?
options: One component's CSS failed to update after a re-render
The API contract used offset-based pagination instead of cursor-based
The boundary between server truth and client truth wasn't drawn clearly, so one component read stale server state while the other read fresh state
The component tree was decomposed into too few boxes
mcqs.explanation: Step 3 exists precisely to prevent two components disagreeing on the same fact — the classic cause is an unclear owner for a piece of server truth, so one reads a cache while the other reads something fresher. Pagination style and box granularity are real concerns from other steps, but not this symptom's usual cause.

mcqs.question: For a live feed, why is a cursor-based pagination endpoint (`?after=<id>`) usually preferred over an offset-based one (`?page=3`)?
options: Cursor-based pagination is always faster for the server to compute
Offset-based pagination cannot be implemented in REST APIs
Cursor-based pagination survives items being inserted or removed mid-list, which offset-based pagination handles by skipping or repeating items
Cursor-based pagination removes the need for a component tree
mcqs.explanation: A live feed keeps inserting new items while a user scrolls; offset-based paging shifts every item's index, so page 3 can silently skip or repeat posts, while a cursor anchored to a specific item's ID isn't affected by inserts before it. It isn't inherently faster server-side, and it has nothing to do with REST support or the component tree.

mcqs.question: A candidate starts writing a `<FeedItem>` component's JSX right after sketching the component tree, before discussing where state lives. What's the risk this framework warns about?
options: JSX cannot be written before an API contract exists, so the code won't compile
The interviewer will assume the candidate doesn't know React
The code will assume a data shape that the not-yet-decided data flow may contradict, forcing a rewrite and burning interview time
Component trees are only a formality and can be skipped entirely
mcqs.explanation: Writing code before agreeing on state ownership means guessing a shape that the later data-flow conversation might invalidate, forcing a backtrack mid-interview. The other options either state a false technical constraint or dismiss a step the framework treats as essential.

mcqs.question: Compared to backend HLD, what does the frontend framework treat as its "hard part" — the thing most likely to be scrutinized as a non-functional concern?
options: Consistency across database replicas
Accessibility and perceived performance, rather than availability and durability
Choosing a consensus algorithm for leader election
Sharding strategy for the primary data store
mcqs.explanation: The comparison table's non-functionals row is the tell: backend HLD leans on availability/durability, while frontend design leans on accessibility, perceived performance, and offline behavior — the concerns a client-side interviewer actually probes. The other three options are backend-side concerns explicitly out of scope for this framework.
